**Abstract.** Education systems count disadvantaged students who achieve highly as a success. We ask how these resilient students rate their own lives. With PISA 2025 data for `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` education systems, we compare resilient students with disadvantaged low achievers in the same school. Resilient students report life satisfaction `r ea("gap","lad:demo")` SD lower. The gap more than doubles, to `r ea("gap","lad:sei")` SD, once socio-emotional skills are held fixed, because resilient students have more such skills. It is negative in `r nneg("gap","lad:sei")` systems and concentrated at the top of the scale. Resilient students are `r ppa("rs","thr:LS10")` percentage points less likely to give the highest answer and barely more likely to give a low one. Response styles do not account for the gap, and coarser answering by low achievers accounts for a minority of it. Resilient students are also `r ea("bench","cell:R:demo")` SD less satisfied than advantaged top achievers, the most satisfied group. School context does not change the gap, and a causal forest finds no variation in it within schools. Indicators of academic resilience should be reported together with students' own evaluations of their lives.

**Keywords:** academic resilience; life satisfaction; subjective wellbeing; socio-emotional skills; PISA; response scales

# Introduction

Education systems are judged in part by their resilient students, the children of the poorest families who score among the best in their country. The OECD reports the share of such students for every system that takes part in PISA, and a body of research asks what schools and countries do to raise it [@agasisti2018]. The indicator records a test score. How these students evaluate their own lives, an outcome that child-indicator research treats as important in its own right [@benarieh2008], is not part of it.

In PISA 2025, resilient students report the lowest life satisfaction of the four groups formed by crossing family background with achievement: `r e("rs","mean:R:LS")` on a scale from 0 to 10, against `r e("rs","mean:PL:LS")` for disadvantaged low achievers and about `r e("rs","mean:AT:LS",1)` for both advantaged groups. Of resilient students, `r pp("rs","mean:R:LS10",0)` per cent give the top answer of 10; among disadvantaged low achievers, `r pp("rs","mean:PL:LS10",0)` per cent do. The difference runs against what their other characteristics predict. Resilient students score `r e("rs","diff:R-PL:SEI")` SD higher on socio-emotional skills than disadvantaged low achievers, and skills are associated with higher life satisfaction.

This paper estimates the gap in life satisfaction between resilient students and the disadvantaged low achievers who attend the same school, in the `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` education systems of PISA 2025 that allow the comparison. Within schools, resilient students report life satisfaction `r ea("gap","lad:demo")` SD lower (SE `r se("gap","lad:demo")`). When we hold their socio-emotional skills fixed, the gap more than doubles, to `r ea("gap","lad:sei")` SD (SE `r se("gap","lad:sei")`). When we also hold fixed their relationships at school and at home, it stays there, at `r ea("gap","lad:full_points")` scale points. The gap is negative in `r nneg("gap","lad:sei")` of `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` systems, significantly so in `r sneg("gap","lad:sei")`, and significantly positive in none.

The gap is concentrated at the top of the scale. With skills held fixed, resilient students are `r ppa("rs","thr:LS10")` percentage points less likely to answer 10, and they are as likely as low achievers to answer 6 or more. A difference of this kind can reflect how students use the scale and how satisfied they are, so we test both. Response styles leave the gap unchanged. Low achievers do answer more coarsely, with an excess of 0s and 5s, and this accounts for `r fm("mix:near:share_explained", 0, scale = 100)` to `r fm("mix:up7:share_explained", 0, scale = 100)` per cent of the shortfall of 10s. Read as a difference in underlying satisfaction, the gap is between `r tm("gop:sei:low", mag = TRUE)` and `r tm("op:sei:top", mag = TRUE)` SD, depending on how much of the difference at the two highest answers reflects a stricter standard for a top answer.

High achievers from advantaged families also report lower life satisfaction than low achievers once skills are held fixed (`r ea("gap","q4:sei")` SD). The penalty among disadvantaged students is larger by `r ea("gap","did:sei")` SD (SE `r se("gap","did:sei")`) in the cross-section, but an instrumental-variable test that uses school-entry cutoffs in `r krow("base","LS_z")$n_sys` systems does not confirm the difference (`r k("lowses","LS_z","gamma:lowSES")`, SE `r kse("lowses","LS_z","gamma:lowSES")`). Against advantaged top achievers, the most satisfied of the four groups, resilient students are `r ea("bench","cell:R:demo")` SD behind, and they remain behind when skills are held fixed, while disadvantaged low achievers do not. The gap does not vary with the status or achievement of schoolmates, with sex or with the expectation of a university degree. A causal forest finds no variation in the gap within schools; linear models suggest that it is smaller for students with a stronger sense of belonging.

The direction of the raw difference has been reported before. In its report on PISA 2018 the OECD notes that, on average across OECD countries, a smaller share of resilient than of other disadvantaged students are satisfied with life [@oecd2019]. That comparison cuts the scale at 7, takes all other disadvantaged students as the reference group, uses no controls and gives no magnitude in the text. The sign reverses in several countries, and the chapter reads the evidence as mildly favourable to resilient students. A second line of work finds an inverted-U relation between life satisfaction and achievement in PISA 2018, with the most satisfied students scoring below the moderately satisfied [@oecd2019b; @li2024]. @siebecke2026 finds the same curve among resilient students in Sweden. That study relates wellbeing to achievement inside the resilient group and does not compare the group's life satisfaction with that of other disadvantaged students. The third relevant literature comes from health research in the United States. Disadvantaged young people who succeed report good psychological adjustment in these studies and carry physiological costs, a pattern known as skin-deep resilience [@brody2013; @miller2015; @chen2022b]. None of these studies measures life satisfaction.

To our knowledge, no earlier study estimates the life-satisfaction gap between resilient students and the disadvantaged low achievers in their own schools. We add three things to the literature above. The first is the comparison itself. Resilient students are set against schoolmates who share their background, in `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` systems, with a magnitude and a standard error. The gap turns out to be nearly uniform (the between-system variance is estimated at zero), where the OECD's descriptive comparison found mixed signs. The second is masking. We know of no study that conditions a gap in wellbeing between high and low achievers on socio-emotional skills, and doing so shows that the raw comparison understates the gap by about half. The third concerns measurement. We locate the gap on the scale and bound how much of it could be a matter of reporting, which bears on any child indicator built on the share of students above a cut point. The result also takes the study of skin-deep resilience to life satisfaction and to countries outside the United States, and it finds there a shortfall in self-reported wellbeing that this literature does not predict.

We use "cost" for a difference between groups of students. The design compares students within schools and does not identify what resilient students would report had they achieved less. @clarke2020 warns against reading differences of this kind as a trade-off between wellbeing and achievement, and on average the two are positively related [@bucker2018; @kaya2021]. Our claim is that disadvantaged students who achieve highly rate their lives at the top of the scale less often than disadvantaged students who do not.

Section 2 sets out the evidence behind four research questions. Section 3 describes the PISA 2025 data, and Section 4 the within-school estimator and the threats to it. Section 5 reports the gap and what skills hide, where on the scale it lies, how resilient students compare with advantaged students, where the gap differs, and the robustness checks. Section 6 discusses what the gap means for academic resilience as an indicator, and Section 7 concludes.

# Background and research questions

Research on academic resilience asks which students, schools and systems produce high achievement against the odds [@agasisti2018]. How the students who achieve it evaluate their lives is a separate question. Four bodies of evidence bear on it, and each leaves one question open.
<!-- The search protocol, logs and evidence table behind this section are in literature/ (scoping_review.md, evidence_table.md, review_structure.md). -->

## Achievement and life satisfaction

On average, students who achieve more are slightly more satisfied with their lives. Two meta-analyses find a small positive correlation between achievement and subjective wellbeing, about 0.16 in the first [@bucker2018; @kaya2021]. A systematic review in *Child Indicators Research* calls the evidence inconsistent [@amholt2020].

The relation is not linear. In PISA 2018, students who answer 9 or 10 score 16 points lower in reading than other students once their socio-economic profile is accounted for, and those who answer 7 or 8 score 15 points higher [@oecd2019b]. The same inverted U appears in mainland China and in Sweden [@li2024; @siebecke2026]. If it holds among disadvantaged students, their high achievers should give fewer of the highest answers.

For disadvantaged students who achieve, the best-developed evidence points the other way. In the studies of skin-deep resilience, young people from poor families who show high competence or self-control have fewer depressive symptoms than their peers, and the cost appears in physical health [@brody2013; @miller2015; @chen2022b]. These studies do not measure life satisfaction, and their physical cost appears mostly in Black and Latinx samples in the United States [@brody2016; @prag2019].

The closest antecedent is the OECD's chapter on resilience and wellbeing in PISA 2018 [@oecd2019]. It compares resilient students with all other disadvantaged students on the share answering 7 or more, without controls. A smaller share of resilient students is satisfied on average across OECD countries and in three systems, and a larger share in three others. The chapter gives no magnitude. A comparison with disadvantaged low achievers in the same schools is missing, and the evidence above predicts different signs for it.

> **RQ1.** Do resilient students report lower life satisfaction than disadvantaged low achievers in the same school, and at which answers does the difference lie?

## What resilient students bring

Resilient students differ from other disadvantaged students in more than test scores. They report more self-efficacy, more motivation to master tasks and a stronger sense of belonging at school [@oecd2019]. In the OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills, high achievers have more of the skills of task performance and open-mindedness, among them persistence and curiosity [@oecd2024]. A growth mindset, the belief that intelligence can be developed, also goes with achievement among poor students: in Chile, students from the poorest families who hold it score as high as much richer students who do not [@claro2016].

The same characteristics are associated with higher life satisfaction. In the OECD Survey on Social and Emotional Skills every skill measured is positively related to it [@oecd2021; @oecd2024]. Among relationships, family support is the strongest correlate of adolescents' life satisfaction across 42 countries and regions [@bi2021], and belonging and freedom from bullying are consistent correlates in PISA and in the Children's Worlds survey [@oecd2019b; @savahl2019].

These two facts imply suppression. If resilient students have more of what raises life satisfaction, a raw comparison with low achievers nets whatever high achievement takes from life satisfaction against what skills and relationships add, and it understates the first. We found no study that holds socio-emotional skills fixed when it compares the wellbeing of high and low achievers, so the size of this masking is unknown.

One qualification limits what PISA 2025 can show. The skills most related to school grades are curiosity, persistence and self-control, and the skills most related to life satisfaction are optimism, trust and emotional regulation [@guo2023; @oecd2021]. PISA 2025 measures six skills of the first kind, so the masking we can estimate is masking by task-oriented skills.

> **RQ2.** How does the gap change when the socio-emotional skills and relationships of resilient students are held fixed?

## Disadvantage among achievers

Lower life satisfaction among high achievers could be general, or it could belong to those who achieve from a poor background. The literature is divided, and most of it concerns adults who have completed a move between social classes.

A larger penalty for disadvantaged achievers has some support. Among German high-school students, achievement is related to life satisfaction only where the mother has at least the education the student is pursuing [@crede2015]. In panel data, upward mobility lowers life satisfaction in the United Kingdom and has no effect in Switzerland [@hadjar2015].

Most quantitative studies find no such penalty. People who move far up fare better on subjective wellbeing than those who stay in the working class in Britain [@chan2018], and in 44 European countries the life satisfaction of the mobile reflects their classes of origin and destination, with nothing added by mobility itself [@dhoore2019]. The cost of achievement pressure has been documented mainly among the affluent, in high-achieving schools [@luthar2020]. @breen2024 argue that a mobility effect is not identified as such and that researchers can instead estimate how the effect of a destination differs by origin. We adopt that form, with high achievement as the destination and family background as the origin.

A second comparison sets disadvantaged achievers against advantaged ones. In the United Kingdom, children from low-income families who were in the top quarter of ability at age 5 are about 0.3 SD less happy at 14 than equally able children from high-income families [@jerrim2025], and competent inner-city adolescents in the United States are more depressed and anxious than competent adolescents from low-stress backgrounds [@luthar1991]. This comparison holds achievement fixed and lets background differ. It includes the general association of family background with life satisfaction, and it shows how far resilient students are from the group that is best placed on both counts.

> **RQ3.** Is the gap specific to disadvantaged students, and how do resilient students compare with high achievers from advantaged families?

## Where the gap may differ

Two mechanisms could make the gap depend on where a resilient student goes to school. The first is comparison with schoolmates. School-average achievement lowers academic self-concept in a 26-country study of 15-year-olds [@marsh2003], and in German panel data high performers in higher-performing classes report lower life satisfaction than high performers elsewhere [@rathmann2018]. The second is status mismatch. Low-income students in the United States show more psychosocial problems as the share of better-off schoolmates rises [@crosnoe2009].

The evidence against is at least as strong. A scoping review finds that low socio-economic position harms wellbeing more in poorer schools [@herke2022], and schools account for only 5 to 9 per cent of the variance in wellbeing indicators in PISA 2015 [@govorova2020].

Sex, aspirations and skills are the remaining candidates. Girls report lower life satisfaction than boys in all 33 countries of one PISA 2015 analysis [@marquez2024]. Unmet educational expectations bring almost no long-term emotional cost once attainment is taken into account [@reynolds2010]. Among skills, self-control predicts fewer depressive symptoms among disadvantaged young people [@miller2015], and for curiosity the literature gives no prediction in either direction. A growth mindset raises the achievement of lower-achieving students in a national experiment in the United States [@yeager2019]. Resilient students also report more self-efficacy and a stronger sense of belonging than other disadvantaged students [@oecd2019]. Whether any of these beliefs and attitudes changes how high achievers evaluate their lives has not been tested. Skills rated by the student call for caution, because self-ratings share reporting habits with the outcome [@guo2023; @lira2022].

We found no study that tests any of these characteristics as a moderator of the relation between achievement and life satisfaction among adolescents. With fourteen candidates and no ranking among them, we examine them jointly.

> **RQ4.** Does the gap vary with the school context, sex, aspirations, mindset or socio-emotional skills of resilient students?

# Data

## Data and sample

We use the public student files of PISA 2025, the OECD's assessment of 15-year-olds enrolled in school [@oecd2026data]. `r N$systems` education systems fielded the life-satisfaction item and at least four of the six socio-emotional skill scales, and they contribute `r big(N$students)` students. Models that compare students within schools need a school identifier in the public file and at least 80 students in each compared group. `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` systems meet both conditions. They contain about `r big(N$R)` resilient students and `r big(N$PL)` disadvantaged low achievers.

## Measures

*Life satisfaction.* Students answer the question "Overall, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?" on a scale from 0 to 10. We analyse the item standardised within each system, where one SD is about 2.3 scale points, and the share of students giving each answer.

*Family background and achievement.* Family background is the PISA index of economic, social and cultural status. Achievement is the reading score, computed separately for each of the ten plausible values. As a check we repeat the main estimates with a composite that gives reading half the weight and mathematics and science a quarter each.

*Socio-emotional skills.* PISA 2025 contains six self-rated scales: perseverance, curiosity, enjoyment of problem-solving, cognitive adaptability, goal setting and self-regulated learning. The skill index is their average. In 17 systems a parent also rates the student's self-regulation.

*Growth mindset.* Students say how far they agree that "you have a certain amount of intelligence, and you really can't do much to change it". Those who disagree or strongly disagree are coded as holding a growth mindset. The item was not fielded in Spain.

*Science self-efficacy and enjoyment of science.* Two scales from the science questionnaire, standardised within system.

*Relationships.* We use four scales: sense of belonging at school, exposure to bullying, family support and feeling safe at school. All scales are standardised within system.

*Scale use.* We build indices of extreme, acquiescent and midpoint responding from 18 questionnaire items unrelated to wellbeing and from the reverse-worded skill items. Students who spent less than one second per questionnaire item are flagged as speeders.

## Groups

Within each system, disadvantaged and advantaged students are the bottom and top quartiles of the status index, and low and top achievers are the bottom and top quartiles of achievement. Resilient students are in the bottom status quartile and the top achievement quartile. @tbl-groups describes the four groups. Resilient students have the lowest mean life satisfaction of the four, and their mean is below that of disadvantaged low achievers in `r csys(rs_sys, "diff:R-PL:LS")` of `r csys(rs_sys, "diff:R-PL:LS", "n")` systems (@fig-means, panel A). Against advantaged students of the same achievement the difference is larger, `r num(row_("rs","mean:AT:LS")$re_mean - row_("rs","mean:R:LS")$re_mean, 2)` scale points, and the mean of resilient students is the lower one in `r cbelow(rs_sys, "mean:R:LS", "mean:AT:LS")` systems (panel B). Top achievers hold a growth mindset far more often than low achievers in both status groups. In both status groups top achievers also answer 10 about half as often as low achievers, and the shares answering 4 or less are almost identical for resilient students and disadvantaged low achievers.

# Empirical approach

## Identification strategy

In each system we estimate, on disadvantaged students in the top or the bottom achievement quartile,

$$y_{is} = \alpha_s + \beta R_{is} + x_{is}'\gamma + \varepsilon_{is},$$

where $y_{is}$ is the standardised life satisfaction of student $i$ in school $s$, $\alpha_s$ is a school fixed effect, $R_{is}$ equals one for resilient students and zero for disadvantaged low achievers, and $x_{is}$ contains sex, age and grade. The gap, $\beta$, compares resilient students with disadvantaged low achievers in the same school. Later specifications add the skill index, the six skills or the relationship scales to $x_{is}$.

We use the final student weights. Standard errors combine the 80 balanced-repeated-replication weights, with Fay's adjustment, and the variation across the ten plausible values. Group membership depends on achievement, so we recompute it for every plausible value and every replicate weight. We pool the system estimates with a random-effects meta-analysis [@dersimonian1986] and report in how many systems the estimate is negative and significant at the 5 per cent level.

*The gap (RQ1).* The answer to RQ1 is $\beta$ with sex, age and grade held fixed. To locate the gap on the scale we estimate the same contrast for the share of students who give each answer from 0 to 10 and for the share at or above each point of the scale.

*Skills and relationships (RQ2).* We add the skill index, then the six skills separately, then the skill index with the four relationship scales, and the skill index with growth mindset. A decomposition that does not depend on the order in which controls enter attributes the change in the gap to each of them [@gelbach2016].

*Disadvantage among achievers (RQ3).* We estimate the contrast between top and low achievers among advantaged students, and the difference between the two gaps in one model. The cross-section cannot rule out that selection into high achievement differs by family background, so we add a test that does not rest on it. In `r krow("base","LS_z")$n_sys` systems a school-entry cutoff places otherwise similar students one grade higher at the time of the test. We use the grade implied by the cutoff and the month of birth as an instrument for the grade attended, with age in months as a linear control [@avvisati2023], and interact the grade with membership of the bottom status quartile. The estimate is the effect of one more grade at a given age. A grade also changes the curriculum and the classmates, so it measures progression through school and not achievement alone. For the second comparison we take the top achievers of the bottom and the top status quartiles and estimate the difference between them, within schools and with the same controls. Advantaged top achievers report the highest life satisfaction of the four groups, so this contrast measures resilient students against the most satisfied group. It holds achievement fixed and lets family background differ, and it therefore includes the general association of background with life satisfaction.

*Heterogeneity (RQ4).* Fourteen characteristics may change the gap, in three groups: the context (the mean status and the mean achievement of schoolmates, each computed without the student, sex, and expecting a university degree), beliefs and attitudes (growth mindset, science self-efficacy, sense of belonging and enjoyment of science) and the six skills. A linear interaction for each characteristic, estimated system by system, imposes a functional form, tests the fourteen separately and without adjustment for one another, and has little power in a single system. We therefore pool the systems, give each the same total weight, and estimate how the gap varies with all fourteen characteristics at once with a causal forest [@wager2018; @athey2019]. Life satisfaction and the resilient indicator are centred within school, so the gap is identified within schools as in the regressions, and both are first adjusted for the fourteen characteristics, age and grade with regression forests. We report three quantities. A calibration test asks whether the forest finds any variation in the gap beyond its average [@chernozhukov2025]. A projection of the gap on the fourteen characteristics shows which of them carry the variation, each adjusted for the others [@semenova2021]. The gap in each fifth of a characteristic shows the shape without a functional form. Being resilient is not a treatment, and the forest describes how a difference between groups varies. For comparison we report the same forest without school fixed effects, the linear counterpart, one model with school fixed effects and all fourteen interactions on the same pooled sample, and the system-by-system interaction models.

## Methodological threats

*Selection.* The gap is a conditional difference between two groups and has no causal interpretation. Students who reach the top quartile from a poor family may differ from those who do not in temperament, ambition or family circumstances that also shape life satisfaction, and life satisfaction may itself affect effort at school. Family background is a minor concern by comparison. The status index correlates only 0.07 with life satisfaction within systems, and both groups come from its bottom quartile. One design rule follows from the role of skills. Skills help to produce achievement, so a top achiever with few skills must have something unobserved in their favour. We therefore never compare high-skill with low-skill students inside the resilient group. Skills enter as controls or as moderators of the contrast between the two groups.

*Schools with both groups.* School fixed effects restrict the comparison to schools that contain both groups. In the median system about two thirds of resilient students attend such a school, and fewer do in systems that track students early, so the within-school estimates rest more on comprehensive systems.
<!-- Two thirds (median 66%) is from the analysis notes in 01_code/README.md, not from the snapshot. -->
We report the estimates without school fixed effects for comparison.

*Inference in the forest.* A forest cannot use the replicate weights. Its standard errors are clustered by school, and because group membership depends on the plausible value we grow the forest once for each of the ten plausible values and combine the results in the same way as the regression estimates. The clustered standard errors do not reflect the stratification of the PISA samples.

*Scale use.* All four questions rest on one self-rated item, and students of different ability may answer it differently. In PISA 2018 the answers 0, 5 and 10 become rarer as mathematics scores rise, which @barringtonleigh2024 reads as less numerate students using only the bottom, middle and top of the scale. Among Czech fifth-graders, the life-satisfaction advantage of pupils with excellent grades grows after correction with anchoring vignettes [@vonkova2019], which points to a stricter standard among high achievers. Four checks ask whether the two groups answer the life-satisfaction item differently. We add the response-style indices as controls and exclude speeders. We estimate a placebo, the gap in choosing 10 on three effort questions with a 1–10 format. We estimate the gap in the share giving each answer from 0 to 10, which detects students who use only the bottom, middle and top of the scale. And we fit an ordered-probit model with a separate shift for resilient students at every threshold of the scale.

*Self-rated skills.* A skill rated by the student may moderate the gap because both ratings share reporting habits. For self-regulated learning we repeat the test with the parent's rating. Curiosity has no second rater, and we test it against the scale-use indices, separate item subsets and the exclusion of speeders.

# Results

## The gap and what skills hide

Resilient students report lower life satisfaction than disadvantaged low achievers in the same school (@tbl-gap). With sex, age and grade held fixed the gap is `r ea("gap","lad:demo")` SD (SE `r se("gap","lad:demo")`). It is negative in `r nneg("gap","lad:demo")` of `r nsys("gap","lad:demo")` systems and significantly negative in `r sneg("gap","lad:demo")`.

| Specification | Gap (SD) | SE | Systems | Negative | Significantly negative |
|:-------------------------------|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|:-----:|
| (1) School fixed effects, sex, age, grade | `r e("gap","lad:demo")` | `r se("gap","lad:demo")` | `r nsys("gap","lad:demo")` | `r nneg("gap","lad:demo")` | `r sneg("gap","lad:demo")` |
| (2) As (1), with the skill index | `r e("gap","lad:sei")` | `r se("gap","lad:sei")` | `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` | `r nneg("gap","lad:sei")` | `r sneg("gap","lad:sei")` |
| (3) As (1), with the six skills | `r e("gap","lad:se6")` | `r se("gap","lad:se6")` | `r nsys("gap","lad:se6")` | `r nneg("gap","lad:se6")` | `r sneg("gap","lad:se6")` |
| (4) As (2), with four relationship scales | `r e("gap","lad:full")` | `r se("gap","lad:full")` | `r nsys("gap","lad:full")` | `r nneg("gap","lad:full")` | `r sneg("gap","lad:full")` |
| (5) As (1), without school fixed effects | `r e("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` | `r se("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` | `r nsys("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` | `r nneg("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` | `r sneg("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` |
| (6) As (2), without school fixed effects | `r e("rs","gap:sei_nofe")` | `r se("rs","gap:sei_nofe")` | `r nsys("rs","gap:sei_nofe")` | `r nneg("rs","gap:sei_nofe")` | `r sneg("rs","gap:sei_nofe")` |

: Life-satisfaction gap between resilient students and disadvantaged low achievers. Each row is a regression of standardised life satisfaction on an indicator for resilient students, estimated in each system on students in the bottom status quartile who are in the top or bottom achievement quartile, and pooled by random effects. Standard errors use 80 replicate weights and ten plausible values. The last column counts systems with a negative estimate significant at 5 per cent; no system has a significantly positive estimate in any row. {#tbl-gap tbl-colwidths="[40,12,12,12,12,12]"}

The gap more than doubles when we hold skills fixed. With the skill index in the model it is `r ea("gap","lad:sei")` SD (SE `r se("gap","lad:sei")`), negative in `r nneg("gap","lad:sei")` systems. The estimate becomes more negative in `r cbelow(gap_sys, "lad:sei", "lad:demo")` of `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` systems (@fig-skills, panel A). Entering the six skills separately gives `r ea("gap","lad:se6")` SD, and adding the relationship scales to the skill index leaves the gap at `r ea("gap","lad:full")` SD, or `r ea("gap","lad:full_points")` scale points. Growth mindset does not account for it either: in the `r nsys("gap","lad:sei_growth")` systems that measure it, the gap with the skill index held fixed is `r ea("gap","lad:sei_gsample")` SD without growth mindset in the model and `r ea("gap","lad:sei_growth")` SD with it. The decomposition attributes the change to what resilient students have more of. Their higher skill index offsets `r e("gap","gel:SEI",3)` SD of the gap, belonging offsets `r e("gap","gel:BELONG_z",3)` and family support `r e("gap","gel:FAMSUP_z",3)`. The raw comparison understates the gap by about half.

To give the size a reference, across all students one SD of the status index is associated with `r e("gap","cont:ESCS")` SD of life satisfaction and one SD of the skill index with `r e("gap","cont:SEI")` SD. The gap with skills held fixed is `r num(abs(row_("gap","lad:sei")$re_mean) / row_("gap","cont:ESCS")$re_mean, 1)` times the first and nearly as large as the second.

The estimates do not depend on the restriction to schools that contain both groups. Without school fixed effects, in `r nsys("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` systems, the gap is `r ea("gap","lad:nofe_demo")` SD before skills are held fixed and `r ea("rs","gap:sei_nofe")` SD after.

The gap is close to uniform across systems (@fig-ranking in the appendix shows every system). The between-system variance is estimated at zero (I² = `r i2("gap","lad:sei")`%), and `r cfunnel(gap_sys, "gap", "lad:sei")` of the `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` system estimates lie within the range that sampling error alone would produce around the pooled mean (@fig-skills, panel B). Because a single system is estimated with a standard error of about `r num(median(gap_sys[term == "lad:sei" & se > 0, se]), 2)` SD, as large as the gap itself, the gap is significant at 5 per cent in only `r csig(gap_sys, "lad:sei")` systems; if every system had the pooled gap, about `r num(sum(pnorm(-1.96 - row_("gap","lad:sei")$re_mean / gap_sys[term == "lad:sei" & se > 0, se])), 0)` would be.

Pooled by world region, the gap with skills held fixed is negative in every region (@fig-regions). It is largest in `r rmin("gap","lad:sei")$region` (`r num(rmin("gap","lad:sei")$re_mean)` SD) and smallest in `r rmax("gap","lad:sei")$region` (`r num(rmax("gap","lad:sei")$re_mean)` SD, SE `r num(rmax("gap","lad:sei")$re_se, 3)`). Against advantaged top achievers every region lies between `r num(rmin("bench","cell:R:demo")$re_mean)` and `r num(rmax("bench","cell:R:demo")$re_mean)` SD.

Panel B: resilient students against advantaged top achievers in the same school, with sex, age and grade held fixed. The black square is the mean of all systems.](`r fig("fig_p8_regions")`){#fig-regions width=100%}


![**Skills hide part of the gap, and the gap is similar everywhere.** System estimates of the within-school gap between resilient students and disadvantaged low achievers. Panel A: the estimate with sex, age and grade held fixed against the estimate that also holds the skill index fixed; under the line of equality the gap is more negative once skills are held fixed. Panel B: each estimate against its standard error, on a log scale, most precise at the top; the funnel is the region in which 95% of estimates would fall if every system had the same gap, equal to the random-effects mean (vertical line). Labels are PISA system codes. The black square marks the random-effects mean of systems.](`r fig("fig_p3_skills")`){#fig-skills width=100%}

## Where on the scale the gap lies

The gap is a difference in the highest answers (@fig-answers). Resilient students answer 10 less often than disadvantaged low achievers in `r cbelow(rs_sys, "mean:R:LS10", "mean:PL:LS10")` of `r csys(rs_sys, "mean:R:LS10", "n")` systems (panel B). With skills held fixed, resilient students are as likely as low achievers to answer 6 or more (a difference of `r pp("rs","thr:LSge6")` percentage points). They are `r ppa("rs","thr:LSge8")` points less likely to answer 8 or more, `r ppa("rs","thr:LSge9")` points less likely to answer 9 or 10, and `r ppa("rs","thr:LS10")` points less likely to answer 10. The missing 10s reappear as 7s, 8s and 9s, which resilient students give more often by `r pp("foc","ans:sei:7")`, `r pp("foc","ans:sei:8")` and `r pp("foc","ans:sei:9")` points. At the other end the difference is small. The share answering 3 or less is `r pp("foc","bin:sei:le3")` points higher among resilient students (SE `r pps("foc","bin:sei:le3")`).

![**The gap lies at the top of the scale.** Panel A: difference between resilient students and disadvantaged low achievers in the same school in the share giving each answer from 0 to 10, in percentage points, with sex, age, grade and the skill index held fixed. Thin lines are systems; the black line and squares are the random-effects mean, with its 95% interval shaded; the vertical axis is cut at −42 and 22 points. Panel B: unadjusted share of each group answering 10 in each system; under the line of equality resilient students answer 10 less often.](`r fig("fig_p4_answers")`){#fig-answers width=100%}

## Disadvantage among achievers

Top achievers from advantaged families also report lower life satisfaction than advantaged low achievers once skills are held fixed (`r esp("gap","q4:sei")`). Before skills are held fixed the two advantaged groups do not differ (`r esp("gap","q4:demo")`). The penalty among disadvantaged students is larger by `r esa("gap","did:sei")` SD with skills held fixed and by `r ea("gap","did:demo")` SD without. Among all students, one SD of achievement is associated with `r ea("gap","cont:ach")` SD lower life satisfaction when skills and status are held fixed. In the cross-section, then, a penalty is attached to high achievement at every level of family background, and it is about twice as large in the bottom quartile as in the top.

The cutoff design does not reproduce the difference. An extra grade at the same age lowers life satisfaction by `r num(abs(krow("base","LS_z")$re_mean), 3)` SD (SE `r kse("base","LS_z")`) on average in the `r krow("base","LS_z")$n_sys` systems with a usable cutoff. The additional effect for students in the bottom status quartile is `r k("lowses","LS_z","gamma:lowSES")` (SE `r kse("lowses","LS_z","gamma:lowSES")`). The interval contains the cross-sectional difference, so the two results do not conflict, but the design that handles selection gives no positive evidence of a larger penalty for disadvantaged students.

Measured against advantaged top achievers, the most satisfied of the four groups, resilient students are much further behind (@fig-benchmark). Within schools, with sex, age and grade held fixed, their life satisfaction is `r ea("bench","cell:R:demo")` SD lower (SE `r se("bench","cell:R:demo")`). The difference is significantly negative in `r csig(bench_sys, "cell:R:demo")` of `r nsys("bench","cell:R:demo")` systems, where the comparison with disadvantaged low achievers is significant in `r sneg("gap","lad:demo")`. Disadvantaged low achievers are `r ea("bench","cell:PL:demo")` SD below advantaged top achievers (SE `r se("bench","cell:PL:demo")`), significantly so in `r csig(bench_sys, "cell:PL:demo")` systems, and advantaged low achievers do not differ from them (`r esp("bench","cell:AL:demo")`). Life satisfaction thus follows family background, and within the disadvantaged group the high achievers are the lower of the two.

Skills change this ranking. Resilient students score `r ea("bench","pair:AT:SEI")` SD lower on the skill index than advantaged top achievers. With the index held fixed they remain `r ea("bench","cell:R:sei")` SD below them (SE `r se("bench","cell:R:sei")`), while disadvantaged low achievers no longer differ from advantaged top achievers (`r esp("bench","cell:PL:sei")`) and advantaged low achievers are above them (`r esp("bench","cell:AL:sei")`). Among students with the same skills, resilient students are the only group that is clearly less satisfied than advantaged top achievers. This contrast includes the general association of family background with life satisfaction, so it measures the distance of resilient students from the most satisfied group and not a cost of achieving.

The last row gives the random-effects mean with its 95% interval.](`r fig("fig_p2_benchmark")`){#fig-benchmark width=100%}

## Where the gap differs

Within schools, the causal forest finds no variation in the gap beyond its average (@fig-forest). The calibration coefficient for variation is `r f_("calib","differential")` (SE `r fse("calib","differential")`), where a forest whose predictions track real differences would give a value near one, and none of the fourteen characteristics has a significant coefficient in the projection of the gap on all of them. The forest's average gap, `r fes("ate","gap")`, is close to the regression estimate. Its power is limited: in a typical plausible value only `r big(mean(finfo$n_sch_both))` of `r big(mean(finfo$n_sch))` schools contain both groups. Without school fixed effects the forest does find variation (calibration coefficient `r f_("calib","differential", model_ = "nofe")`, SE `r fse("calib","differential", model_ = "nofe")`), and the projection attributes it mainly to sense of belonging (`r fesp("blp","BELONG", model_ = "nofe")` per SD).

![**The gap at each level of fourteen characteristics.** Causal-forest estimates of the within-school gap between resilient students and disadvantaged low achievers in each fifth of a continuous characteristic, or in each category of an indicator, pooled over all systems, with 95% intervals. The dotted line is the forest's average gap. Schoolmates' status and achievement are computed without the student.](`r fig("fig_p5_forest")`){#fig-forest width=100%}

The linear models point in the same direction as the forest without fixed effects. In one within-school model with all fourteen interactions on the pooled sample, each SD of sense of belonging makes the gap smaller by `r fes("ols","BELONG")` and a growth mindset by `r fes("ols","growth")`, while each SD of curiosity makes it larger by `r num(abs(frow("ols","CURIO")$est))` (SE `r fse("ols","CURIO")`) and of science self-efficacy by `r num(abs(frow("ols","EFFSCIE")$est))` (SE `r fse("ols","EFFSCIE")`). The system-by-system interaction models agree (@fig-interactions in the appendix). With a Bonferroni threshold for fourteen tests, belonging (`r esp("mech","mod:BELONG:topX")`), self-regulated learning (`r esp("mech","mod:SELFREG:topX")`) and curiosity (`r esp("mech","mod:CURIO:topX")`) pass, and enjoyment of science (`r esp("mech","mod:JOYSCIE:topX")`) is at the threshold.

The context does not change the gap. Per SD of schoolmates' mean status the gap changes by `r es("mech","mod:schESCS:topX")`, and per SD of schoolmates' mean achievement by `r es("mech","mod:schACH:topX")`. The difference between girls and boys is `r es("mech","mod:female:topX")`, and between students who do and do not expect a university degree `r es("mech","mod:uni:topX")`. Across systems, mean life satisfaction, the share answering 10, school segregation by status and mean achievement do not predict the size of the gap. Two candidate channels account for none of it either. Resilient students have more science self-efficacy (`r e("mech","acc:gamma:EFFSCIE_z")` SD) and are `r pp("mech","acc:gamma:uni",0)` points more likely to expect a university degree, but when we add both, with a measure of career clarity, the gap moves from `r e("mech","acc:base",3)` to `r e("mech","acc:full",3)`.

The self-regulation result does not hold with a second rater. In the 17 systems with a parent questionnaire (`r big(N$parR)` resilient students), the interaction is `r ob("noach:ols_student:topXSR")` (SE `r ob("noach:ols_student:topXSR", what = "se")`) with the student's own rating and `r ob("noach:ols_parent:topXSR")` (SE `r ob("noach:ols_parent:topXSR", what = "se")`) with the parent's rating of the same skill. The parent sample is too small to exclude an effect of the original size, but its point estimate is zero.

The curiosity result holds within the student questionnaire. The interaction stays between `r e("cur","purged",3)` and `r e("cur","joint:CURIO",3)` when we add the response-style indices and their interactions, purge curiosity of response style, drop speeders or enter all six skills together. The reverse-worded curiosity item alone gives the same sign, though a smaller and insignificant interaction (`r esp("cur","items:rev")`). Curiosity works at the lower end of the scale: each SD raises the share of resilient students answering 4 or less by `r pp("cur","ladder:LSle4")` points relative to low achievers and leaves the share answering 10 unchanged (`r pp("cur","ladder:LS10")` points). A weaker interaction of the same sign appears among advantaged top achievers (`r esp("cur","q4")`). All moderators other than self-regulated learning rest on self-report alone, and no second rater exists for curiosity or belonging.

## Robustness

*Measure of achievement.* With achievement measured by the composite weighted towards reading, the gap is `r ea("gapw","lad:demo")` SD with sex, age and grade held fixed (SE `r se("gapw","lad:demo")`) and `r ea("gapw","lad:sei")` SD with the skill index also held fixed (SE `r se("gapw","lad:sei")`), against `r ea("gap","lad:demo")` and `r ea("gap","lad:sei")` SD with reading. Resilient students defined on the composite are `r ea("benchw","cell:R:demo")` SD below advantaged top achievers (SE `r se("benchw","cell:R:demo")`). With the skill index held fixed, the gap is `r ea("gaps","lad:sei")` SD (SE `r se("gaps","lad:sei")`) when achievement is measured by science and `r ea("gapa","lad:sei")` SD (SE `r se("gapa","lad:sei")`) by the simple average of mathematics, reading and science. Resilient students report lower life satisfaction under every measure.

*Response style and careless answering.* With the indices of extreme, acquiescent and midpoint responding in the model the gap is `r ea("rs","gap:sei_rs")` SD, against `r ea("rs","gap:sei_rssample")` in the same sample without them. Without speeders it is `r ea("rs","gap:sei_nospeed")` SD.

*Avoiding the top of any numeric scale.* On two of the three effort questions resilient students choose 10 about as often as low achievers (differences of `r pp("rs","plac:EFF1_10")` and `r pp("rs","plac:EFFQ_10")` points), and on the third they choose it `r pp("rs","plac:EFF2_10")` points more often.

*Coarse answering.* Resilient students answer 5 less often by `r ppa("foc","ans:sei:5")` points and 0 less often by `r ppa("foc","ans:sei:0")`, answers for which a difference in satisfaction predicts nothing. @barringtonleigh2024 describes the same pattern in PISA 2018. If the excess of 5s measures the students who use only 0, 5 and 10, they are `r fm("mix:near:s_PL", 0, scale = 100)` per cent of disadvantaged low achievers and close to none of the resilient students. When we remove their answers, coarse answering accounts for `r fm("mix:near:share_explained", 0, scale = 100)` to `r fm("mix:up7:share_explained", 0, scale = 100)` per cent of the shortfall of 10s, depending on how these students round. Resilient students remain `r ppa("foc","bin:sei:ge8")` points less likely to answer 8 or more, a comparison that rounding to the nearest of the three values does not affect.

*A stricter standard for a top answer.* Resilient students may require more of their lives before they answer 9 or 10. PISA 2025 has no anchoring vignettes and no second wellbeing measure, so we cannot separate such a standard from lower satisfaction. The ordered-probit model bounds it. If the whole difference at the two highest thresholds is a matter of reporting, the gap in underlying satisfaction is `r tm("gop:sei:low", mag = TRUE)` SD. If none of it is, the gap is `r tm("op:sei:top", mag = TRUE)` SD.

# Discussion

## Findings and interpretation

Disadvantaged students who achieve highly are less satisfied with their lives than disadvantaged schoolmates who do not. The usual comparisons hide the difference in two ways. Their skills and relationships offset half of it. The rest disappears at conventional cut points. At 7 or more on the scale, the threshold the OECD uses for a satisfied student, the gap is `r ppa("foc","bin:sei:ge7")` percentage points, against `r ppa("rs","thr:LS10")` at the top answer. These two features may explain why the OECD's comparison for PISA 2018, which used that cut point and no controls, found a small difference with mixed signs [@oecd2019], while we find a gap of one sign in nine systems out of ten.

The result agrees with the inverted-U relation between life satisfaction and achievement. In PISA 2018 the highest reading scores belong to students who answer 7 or 8 [@oecd2019b]. Resilient students give those answers in place of 10. Our estimates show the curve from the side of achievement, within one status group and within schools. They also show that it is not confined to the poor. Advantaged top achievers give fewer top answers than advantaged low achievers once their skills are held fixed.

The relation to skin-deep resilience is less direct than the sign suggests. Those studies find fewer depressive symptoms among disadvantaged young people who succeed [@brody2013; @miller2015], and we find lower life satisfaction. But resilient students in PISA are barely more likely than low achievers to give a low answer, which is the part of the scale closest to distress. They less often give their lives the highest evaluation. A group can be free of symptoms and still stop short of complete satisfaction, so the two sets of results may describe the same young people on different outcomes.

Our data cannot settle what a shortfall of top answers means. One reading is lower satisfaction, perhaps because achievement raises aspirations. In adults, aspirations offset part of the happiness return to education [@clark2015; @ferrante2009], and the people most successful in education and income sit slightly below the top of the happiness scale [@oishi2007]. A second reading is a stricter standard. Reference points for life satisfaction rise with education [@kristoffersen2018], and adolescents with higher-achieving peers hold higher standards when they rate themselves [@lira2022]. The third, coarser answering by low achievers, is the one we could test, and it accounts for a minority of the shortfall. The bounds of `r tm("gop:sei:low", mag = TRUE)` and `r tm("op:sei:top", mag = TRUE)` SD describe what remains uncertain. If the first reading is right the shortfall matters, because very high life satisfaction in adolescence is associated with better psychosocial functioning than average life satisfaction [@suldo2006].

The absence of moderation by context runs against the two mechanisms with the clearest support in earlier work, comparison with higher-achieving classmates [@rathmann2018] and the position of a poor student among better-off schoolmates [@crosnoe2009]. It agrees with the small share of the variance in wellbeing that lies between schools [@govorova2020]. The gap is close to uniform, and the causal forest finds no variation in it within schools. Where linear models do find some, it runs through belonging: resilient students who feel they belong at school are closer to their low-achieving schoolmates. Curiosity and science self-efficacy go the other way, and the self-regulation moderator vanished when a parent rated the skill. All of these rest on self-report, and they are best read as leads for designs that can test them.

## Implications for indicators of resilience

Academic resilience is reported as a success of education systems. It should be reported with what resilient students say about their lives. An indicator defined as the share of students above a cut point can also miss a difference between groups that lies above the cut. Reporting the share at the highest answers next to the share of satisfied students would show it.

## Limitations

These conclusions have limits. The data are a cross-section, and the gap is a difference between groups that may differ in unobserved ways. The outcome is a single item. PISA 2025 measures task-oriented skills, so we cannot say whether optimism or emotional regulation would mask more of the gap or explain part of it. And the research questions were formulated while we explored these data, so the results await replication.

# Conclusion

In `r nsys("gap","lad:sei")` education systems, students from the poorest quarter of families who reach the top quarter of achievement rate their lives lower than poor schoolmates at the bottom of the achievement distribution. The difference is `r ea("gap","lad:demo")` SD in a direct comparison and `r ea("gap","lad:sei")` SD between students with the same socio-emotional skills. It consists mostly of fewer answers of 10. Of the four groups formed by background and achievement, resilient students are the least likely to give their lives the highest rating. We find no sign that schoolmates, sex or aspirations change the gap, and response styles do not produce it.

Systems that count resilient students as a success have reason to ask those students how their lives are going and to look at the top of the scale when they do. The finding gives no argument for expecting less of disadvantaged students, and it does not establish that achievement harms them.

Two additions to the data would decide between the readings that remain open. A PISA cycle with anchoring vignettes for life satisfaction, or with a second wellbeing measure, would separate a stricter standard from lower satisfaction. A cycle that measures optimism, stress resistance and emotional control beside the skills of PISA 2025 would show whether the skills most tied to life satisfaction mask the gap further or account for it.
